transcript:
Header: 2025-03-11 15:30 PT | Duration ~72m | Recording generated by Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Samira Cho (Redwood AE), Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Infra), Anika Rao (Helios SRE), Derek Lin (Helios ML Eng), Jason Park (Helios CTO), Lina Gomez (Helios Platform), Oliver (intern)

Summary: quick deep dive into GPU runtime perf profiling. Focus areas: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM throughput/latency tradeoffs, CUDA Graphs and warmup, KV-cache evictions, batching strategies, quantization effects on kernel choice, and implications for VPC/on-prem Dedicated runs.

00:00 Samira (AE): okay folks thanks for joining, we were told there was a heavy perf question set from Helios after your initial POC runs, so Miguel and Priya are here to do a deep dive into the GPU runtime stuff.
02:15 Miguel (SE): cool yeah, quick agenda: show microbenchmarks, kernel selection notes (cuBLAS/cuDNN vs custom CUDA kernels), compare TensorR-T LLM flows to v-llm baseline, talk about CUDA Graph warmup and reuse, then open Q&A.
04:02 Derek (ML Eng): quick context — we're running a 8xA100 DGX-ish setup on-prem, model is a 30B decoder-only, mixed precision fp16, we saw big variance in p99 depending on batch mixing and prompt lengths.
05:30 Priya (Infra): key ask from infra is predictability for our 99th pct latency; costs less of a first-class for now but capacity planning matters.
06:10 Miguel: first slide — kernel selection. so runtime inspects layer shapes + sequence length distribution, picks gemm kernels from cuBLAS when matmul shapes are rectangular-ish, but for small head sizes or quantized kernels we sometimes prefer fused custom kernels - those are the ones that reduce launch overhead and improve memory reuse.
08:45 Anika (SRE): when you say fused kernels, are those the ones Redwood maintains or from TensorRT?
09:05 Miguel: good Q — two sources: TensorRT's LLM plugins (they produce fused attention/matmul kernels) and our runtime's custom fused kernels for small-seq or KV-cache heavy workloads. TensorR-T's plugins are great for throughput on fixed sequence lengths, but they can be brittle for dynamic batching and KV cache reuse patterns.
11:20 Miguel: we noticed in our tests TensorR-T LLM pipeline gave ~1.6x throughput on steady-state long sequences (1024) but worse tail latencies when you have hotpath cache hits + eviction churn. vLLM-based approach (server process + sharding) has better single-request p95 due to better cache locality but lower peak throughput in some of our synthetic bursts.
13:50 Jason (CTO): can you clarify v-llm — do you mean the approach using a Python server with memory pinned caches? we thought v-llm was more of an open source serving runtime.
14:10 Miguel: yes, sorry mispronouncing — v-llm is the OSS project; it's memory-friendly and uses continuous batching heuristics but depends heavily on CPU-GPU copy overlap. TensorR-T LLM (we'll say TRT-LLM) offloads more into optimized CUDA kernels and sometimes CUDA graphs.
15:35 Samira: transcription note — we'll share the kernel-level profiles; we've got snapshots from Nsight and also perf counters from the CUDA profiling tools.
17:00 Miguel: the critical thing is kernel selection heuristics tie into quantization: int8/4 uses different GEMM paths (TensorCores with INT8 throughput) which often force us into TensorRT kernels because cuBLAS fused paths don't always support sparsity or custom quant kernels. In our bench, int8 gave 2.3x token/sec vs fp16 but accuracy drift for your evaluation prompts was nontrivial; so it's a trade.
20:40 Derek: we saw a weird memory fragmentation issue when we enabled prefix caching — after ~4k requests GPU memory fragmented and kernel launch times spiked.
21:15 Priya: yep we've observed that — is that something Redwood's allocator handles?
21:45 Miguel: Redwood runtime has a multi-bucket allocator and does periodic compaction heuristics. On Dedicated we can enable a sticky allocation policy to avoid cross-request fragmentation but that increases memory headroom. For on-prem you can opt to force a pre-allocated KV slab to lock addresses.
24:30 Anika: what's the impact of CUDA graphs here? we've tried to record a few graphs but see little benefit unless the input shapes are highly stable.
25:05 Miguel: exactly — CUDA graphs help remove launch overhead and kernel scheduling jitter. They shine when you can capture a stable execution graph (same batch shape, same sequence length). But with dynamic prompts and variable sequence lengths, graph capture/instantiate/launch cost sometimes negates benefit; Redwood's runtime can auto-fallback between graph and non-graph paths.
27:50 Samira: any practical tips for Helios?
28:10 Miguel: two practical knobs: 1) normalize prompt chunk sizes to reduce shape variance — pad to bucked lengths e.g., 128/256/512 instead of letting them flow, 2) maintain a small pool of prewarm graphs for top-10 common shapes and route requests accordingly.
30:00 Derek: what about KV cache eviction strategies? our POC had cache thrash when we had many short conversations mixed with long ones.
31:00 Miguel: we recommend LRU by conversation-id with per-GPU quotas and optional prefix-sharing for multi-turn sessions. Another pattern: keep a small hot set cached and push long-tail to cold-storage (CPU memory) with async prefetch when conversation resumes. That reduces GPU memory pressure at some latency cost.
33:45 Miguel: also important: embedding large KV values as compressed half-precision with quantization-friendly layouts can reduce memory ~30% with small perf penalty when you decode in-stream.
36:10 Anika: curious about interconnects — when you shard across multiple GPUs, do you rely on NCCL for KV sync? we saw stalls.
36:35 Priya: latency spikes looked correlated with NCCL allreduce during cache syncs.
36:50 Miguel: we use NCCL for weight updates and sharded KV syncs; for inference KV we avoid global allreduce by using sharded routing so each request hits the GPU that owns the KV. When cross-GPU compaction is needed we do staggered background syncs to avoid synchronous NCCL ops on hot paths.
39:20 Derek: benchmark numbers? you mentioned 1.6x TRT-LLM throughput on long seqs earlier — can you share numbers for mixed prompt workloads?
39:45 Miguel: yes — summary from our internal microbench (30B model on A100):
- steady long seq (1024): TRT-LLM throughput = 1.6x vLLM baseline, p95 comparable
- mixed short (avg 64) + occasional long bursts: vLLM had 10-15% better p99, TRT had higher median throughput but worse tail due to graph cache misses
- int8 quant: +2.0-2.4x throughput vs fp16 but p50->p99 variance increased and hallucination risk rose per your eval prompts
- CUDA graphs prewarm: if you have top-5 shapes covered, graphs reduce median latency by ~18% and p95 by ~12% for those shapes

43:10 Jason: what instrumentation should we provide to get close to these numbers in our environment?
43:35 Miguel: two things: (1) your real prompt trace (JSON array with timestamps, shapes) — we asked for 50 sample prompts but 1k would be better, and (2) a representative model checkpoint (or config + weight bits) so we can run deterministic microbenchmarks. Also, enable GPU perf counters (sm_efficiency, achieved_occupancy, l2_hit) and a small nsight timeline capture for a sample long-run.
45:50 Derek: do we need to open any ports for Nsight on our VPC? security-wise that's a concern.
46:10 Samira: we can do initial profiling in Redwood Dedicated infra if you'd rather not open Nsight on-prem. For on-prem VPC we can run a short instrumented job that only exports anonymized perf counters; we avoid sending raw weights off-site.
47:25 Priya: any known limitations with CUDA 12.x vs 11.x for TRT-LLM plugins?
47:40 Miguel: yes CUDA 12 changed some driver-level scheduling — TRT-LLM plugins are moving fast; some vendor kernels were optimized for 11.x and require recompile for 12.x. Our runtime supports both but recommends homogeneous driver stack across nodes and matching the TensorRT plugin build.
49:55 Anika: can you expand on kernel launch overheads? our logs show many small kernels and high kernel launch CPU-side time.
50:20 Miguel: small kernels incur high overhead because GPU drivers serialize launches or consume CPU cycles for each kernel. Strategies: fuse more ops into single kernel, use CUDA graphs to amortize launch cost, move more to TensorCores fusion paths, and use persistent kernels for attention loops. Persistent kernels stay resident and iterate on tokens with minimal host intervention.
52:30 Derek: are persistent kernels compatible with KV cache patterns?
52:48 Miguel: partially — persistent kernels are great for autoregressive generation loops but you need to handle KV read/write carefully; Redwood runtime manages that by mapping KV buffers into persistent kernel address space and providing atomic token append primitives. It's tricky but helps with latency.
55:10 Lina (Platform): for our security reviews we need to understand where the perf telemetry lives — is it sent to Redwood?
55:30 Samira: we only request anonymized counters unless you opt-in to deeper traces; for Dedicated we can keep telemetry in your VPC and only exchange aggregate reports. We'll include this in the security docs.
56:40 Miguel: quick note on quantization and kernel choice — for int4/int8 you often need custom lowering and integer GEMM kernels; many of those are in TensorRT or vendor-supplied libs. Our runtime has a fallback to simulated int ops on fp16 paths if the vendor kernel set is missing, which trades latency for correctness.
59:30 Derek: can you speak to how batching strategy affects p99? we saw batching reduce median but sometimes blow up tail.
59:50 Miguel: yes — large batch windows increase throughput but add queuing latency for some requests. Redwood supports latency-aware batching where we prioritize oldest requests or high-priority tokens and allow small reserved pools so some requests skip batching. That keeps p99 bounded. Also dynamic batch trimming helps during bursts.
62:20 Anika: one last practical — our ops team wants a cookbook: minimal runtime config for stable p99 under mixed traffic.
62:40 Miguel: we'll provide a cookbook: recommended default -- enable sticky allocator, prewarm top-5 CUDA graphs, set quantization to fp16 fallback with auto-int8 trial on staging, KV LRU with per-GPU quotas, and latency-aware batching with 50ms max queue. We'll attach it.
64:00 Samira: to wrap up — next steps and we listed action items. Thanks all.
